newsitem.title: USA: Wal-Mart breaks from tradition at annual meeting.
newsitem.headline: Wal-Mart breaks from tradition at annual meeting.

text.p: The carnival atmosphere was gone and a parade of celebrities and sports stars was noticeably absent as retailer Wal-Mart Stores Inc. broke from tradition Friday at its annual meeting here.

Fitness guru Richard Simmons warmed up a crowd of 15,000 shareholders and employees with an aerobic dance sequence, and country singer Pam Tillis belted out the national anthem in a packed sports arena on the University of Arkansas campus.

But after that, it was all business as executives of the world's largest retailer spelled out expansion plans and shareholders rejected a proposal that Wal-Mart take steps to avoid another round of embarrassing disclosures over the use of child labour by some of its vendors.

Talk show host Kathy Lee Gifford, who was caught up last year in allegations sweatshops hired children at meagre wages to make some of her Wal-Mart clothing line, was not even invited to this year's meeting, executives said.

"Earlier in the week, we had several sports stars, models and singers, and on Thursday night we had a concert with (country singers) Leann Rimes and Travis Tritt, but the tone of this meeting was focused on business," spokesman Dale Ingram said.

Wal-Mart annual meetings, long hosted by founder Sam Walton, traditionally were raucous affairs featuring light shows and a massive vendor fair that drew celebrities and sports stars hawking Wal-Mart lines.

But company executives said the toned-down meeting did not mean the glory days of the retailing giant were behind them. Wal-Mart stock closed Friday at a 52-week high of $31.375 a share in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange, fuelled by higher profit margins and forecasts of continued robust worldwide growth.

"Our return on assets went up for the first time in several years, and we reduced our interest expense $43 million over last year," Chief Financial Officer John Menzer said. "Our average customer spent $384 last year with us. ... We know that can only go higher."

Wal-Mart, which pioneered mega-marketing, operates 3,000 stores worldwide and controls 7 percent of the U.S. retail market. The Bentonville, Ark.-based retailer plans to add 50 new U.S. discount stores and 100 new supercenters this year. Up to 35 new stores also are planned for Mexico, Canada, Argentina, Brazil, Puerto Rico, China and Indonesia.

Les Copeland, senior manager of internal corporate affairs, said it was "not unreasonable" to expect Wal-Mart's international division to match forecasts of $400 million in retail sales in fiscal 1998, up 32 percent over last year.

"We made $24 million in profits in Canada and Mexico last year, and the first quarter this year we showed a $6 million profit vs. the $16 million loss we suffered during the same period last year," Copeland said.
The international division is responsible for less than 5 percent of Wal-Mart's overall retail sales but is poised for strong growth in the years ahead, he said.

"We are building companies in these countries, and we are building a brand name," Copeland said. "In China alone, there are 1.2 billion consumers, and we have a retail business that offers low prices and the goods people want. As we learn what customers want, we are finding success."

As a map of the world flashed across eight giant television screens in the sports arena, Bob Martin, president of Wal-Mart's international division, highlighted expansion opportunities in Latin America, China and Indonesia.
"As I was coming here today, I realised that somewhere in the world there is always a Wal-Mart open for business," he said. "And I believe everybody deserves the right to shop in a Wal-Mart store."
